transcript.text: Hi, our integrated fridge freezer (behind a kitchen door) - the fridge is around 10 degrees but the freezer seems ok. We had a power cut a week ago, not sure if related. Rented flat, can't really take it out.

A warm fridge with a cold freezer usually points to an airflow issue rather than a lack of cooling power. In frost-free models, a fan pushes cold air from the freezer into the fridge; if that fan fails or the air path is blocked by food or ice, the fridge warms up while the freezer stays cold. Please check if any items are blocking the vents at the back of the fridge section and listen to see if you can hear a fan running inside the fridge compartment when the door is closed.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.
I can't see any vent at the back of the fridge, so I'm not sure. I can hear it running a lot, but I can't tell if there's a fan. No burning smell and nothing tripping.

It sounds like you have a sealed unit where the cooling coils are hidden behind the rear panel. The fact that the freezer is cold but the fridge is warm suggests that cold air isn't circulating from the freezer into the fridge section, which usually happens when ice blocks the internal vents or the fan pushing the air has failed. To distinguish between these two, we need to check for ice build-up. Please switch the appliance off at the wall socket and leave both doors open for 24 hours to fully defrost it.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.

Ok. I'd have to empty everything out of both sides to do that, and the freezer is fine so I'd rather not lose the food. Is there anything else I can check first? There's some frost on the back of the freezer but not loads.

Yes, there are two non-invasive checks you can do first. First, please check if any food items are pressed against the back wall of the fridge compartment; even a small blockage here stops cold air from entering. Second, with the door closed and the appliance running, listen carefully inside the fridge section for a faint humming or whirring sound (the evaporator fan). If you hear this but the fridge is still warm, it suggests airflow is blocked by ice behind the panel rather than a failed fan. If you don't hear any fan noise at all, the fan motor itself may have failed.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.

I can't tell what's at the back of the fridge, I don't know if there's any food touching it. I can hear it running a lot but can't tell if any of that is a fan inside the fridge. Anything else I can try without emptying it all?

Since you can't easily see inside or empty the freezer, let's try one quick check that often solves this without moving food. In many integrated models, a small drain hole at the bottom of the fridge compartment lets defrost water escape; if this blocks with debris or ice, it can freeze up and block the air path to the fridge. If you see standing water or debris there, try clearing it gently with warm water or a soft pipe cleaner. Let me know if that was blocked or clear.
I can't see any drain hole or standing water in the fridge, but I'm not sure where it would be. Is there anything else I can check, or should I just report it to the letting agent?

Given that you cannot safely access the internal components to clear ice or test the fan, and the fridge is significantly warm while the freezer is cold, this points to a failed defrost component (such as the heater or thermostat) causing an internal blockage. This is not something that can be fixed without dismantling the appliance behind the kitchen panels. You should report this to your letting agent as a repair issue; they will need to arrange for an engineer to diagnose and replace the faulty part.
